meaning: Mythological weaver who was transformed into a spider

phonemes.desc: Aspirated rho plus acute on short alpha [rákʰ] — the pitch peak and the root of 'spider'.
Kappa-nu-eta [knɛː]; the -χνη ending is the same root seen in ἀράχνης, 'spider'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-RAH-knay' — the middle syllable is stressed and higher-pitched; the final -ē is long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἀράχνη (arákhnē), 'spider' and the name of the Lydian weaver

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: Possible root *reh₂g- 'to weave' or *h₂erh₃- 'to spin'; etymology disputed

pronunciation.note: Arachnē is Tier 1 because the Greek ἀράχνη contains both stress (acute on the short alpha of the second syllable, associated with long-final pattern) and length (final η). The aspirated rho is preserved in the classical spelling.

domains.title: The Weaver Transformed
domains.subtitle: Weaving, Hubris, Metamorphosis
domains.lead: Arachnē is the Lydian maiden whose weaving rivaled a goddess's and who was transformed into the first spider. Her myth is a meditation on skill, pride, and the dangerous boundary between human excellence and divine honor.

cards.name: Master Weaver
cards.desc: Her tapestries were so fine that nymphs left their streams to watch her work.

cards.name: Rival of Athena
cards.desc: She challenged Athena to a contest and wove the gods' scandals with flawless skill.

cards.name: The Spider
cards.desc: Transformed into the first arachnid, she kept her gift but lost her human form.

cards.name: Loom as Arena
cards.desc: The contest of weaving becomes a contest over who may speak truth about the gods.

symbols.name: Loom
symbols.meaning: The site of her contest with Athena and the instrument of her fame

symbols.name: Spider web
symbols.meaning: The eternal trace of her transformed body and her unceasing craft

symbols.name: Hanging thread
symbols.meaning: Arachne's attempted suicide by hanging, interrupted by Athena's metamorphosis

symbols.name: Tapestry of divine scandals
symbols.meaning: Her impious but accurate portrayal of Zeus's seductions and deceptions

mythology.lead: Arachnē's myth turns on a contest of representation. She is not punished for bad weaving but for weaving too well — and for choosing a subject that shames the gods.

myths.title: The Challenge
myths.text: Arachnē, a Lydian maiden, boasted that her skill surpassed Athena's. The goddess appeared as an old woman and warned her to repent. When Arachnē refused, Athena revealed herself and proposed a contest. Athena wove the glory of the gods; Arachnē wove their thefts and betrayals — Europa, Leda, Danaë, and others wronged by Olympian desire.

myths.title: The Transformation
myths.text: Athena could find no flaw in Arachnē's work, yet its impiety enraged her. She struck the maiden, who hanged herself in shame. In pity or punishment, Athena sprinkled her with Hekate's herb and transformed her into a spider, condemning her and her descendants to weave forever.

myths.title: Weaving as Speech
myths.text: The contest is one of the great myths about art itself. Arachnē's tapestry is 'true' but dangerous; Athena's is official but sanitized. The myth asks whether skill grants the right to tell forbidden truths, and whether divine power can tolerate accurate criticism.

lore.syncretism: Arachnē has few direct non-Greek parallels, but the motif of the transformed weaver appears in many traditions. The Greeks themselves gave her name to the spider class Arachnida. In Roman and Renaissance art she becomes an emblem of human artistry and its risks. Modern biology still uses 'arachnid' for spiders, scorpions, and mites, preserving her metamorphosis in scientific Latin.
lore.culturalLegacy: Arachne's name lives in the word 'arachnid' and in every spiderweb glistening with dew. She is the patron spirit of artists who challenge authority, of women whose skill threatens the powerful, and of the punished genius. In feminist readings she is a victim of divine jealousy; in cautionary readings, a warning against hubris. Both readings agree on one point: her art was unforgettable.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Arachnē is the artist as transgressor. Her fingers knew what her tongue could not safely say. The loom became her printing press, her courtroom, her rebellion. Athena did not destroy the tapestry; she destroyed the weaver — a sign that the work itself could not be answered.

The transformation into a spider is ambiguous. Is it punishment or preservation? Arachnē loses her human form but keeps her gift, weaving now without rivalry, without audience, without end. In that ceaseless making there is something like immortality, and something like loneliness. She is every creator whose excellence outruns their place.
lore.archaeology: The myth of Arachnē was extremely popular in Roman wall painting and on sarcophagi, where the contest and transformation appear repeatedly. Greek vase painting more often shows Athena with weaving women than the specific Arachnē scene. Spiders and their webs appear as decorative motifs in Byzantine and Renaissance art, often carrying the moral weight of the myth.
